About

Hi! I’m Matthew Scicluna, a PhD student in bioinformatics at the Université de Montréal, with a background in machine learning, statistics, and mathematics.

My current research focuses on the representation of genetic data — essentially, how we can compress information from millions of genomes into lower-dimensional representations without losing too much information. I am particularly interested in embedding these data in two dimensions for visualization.

I develop methods and diagnostics that make dimensionality reduction more trustworthy, including manifold-learning algorithms that scale to biobank-sized datasets and attribution techniques that explain what an embedding is actually showing.

Along the way I have worked on deep learning for microscopy at insitro, neuro-symbolic visual question answering at Huawei’s Noah’s Ark Lab, interpretability for genomic deep-learning models at the Montreal Heart Institute, and manifold learning for population structure as a visiting fellow in the Krishnaswamy Lab at Yale Genetics.

The PHATE plot below shows a three-dimensional representation of 4,094 individuals, based on approximately 170,000 SNPs from HGDP+1KGP — the harmonized, open-access callset that joins the Human Genome Diversity Project to the 1000 Genomes Project, covering 78 populations worldwide (Koenig et al., Genome Research, 2024).

Selected research

Visualizing population structure at biobank scale

manuscript in preparation — available on request

How neighborhood-scale hyperparameters decide whether genuine ancestry structure — rather than sampling artifacts — appears in PHATE, t-SNE, and UMAP embeddings of population-genetic data. Shown across HGDP+1KGP, the UK Biobank, and All of Us, and validated on synthetic branching benchmarks. I led the study and its biobank analyses, built the genetics preprocessing and analysis pipeline, and contributed a scalable random-landmark PHATE implementation upstream.

Transparent deep learning for genomic ancestry prediction

American Journal of Human Genetics, 2026

A transparent and generalizable deep-learning framework for ancestry prediction from genotypes. I ran the interpretability and attribution experiments and wrote the first full draft of the manuscript.

Code

  • DIETNETWORK contributor 3 stars · 2 forks

    The model code behind the paper: the ancestry-prediction network, its training pipeline, and the attribution experiments I ran. Led by Camille Rochefort-Boulanger.

Attributions for dimensionality reduction

Bioinformatics Advances, 2023

t-SNE tells you where each cell or genome lands, but not why. This work adds gradient-based feature attributions to t-SNE so you can see which input features drive each point's position — making a non-linear embedding interpretable. Implemented as an open-source Python/Cython package and evaluated on single-cell RNA-seq, SARS-CoV-2 genomes, and image benchmarks.

Code

  • interpretable-tsne author 1 star · 2 forks

    Gradient-based attributions for t-SNE, as a Python/Cython package extending scikit-learn. Still tested and patched years after the paper it was published with.
